newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea pumps money into banks after Hanbo crisis.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea pumps money into banks after Hanbo crisis.

text.p: South Korea's central bank on Monday pumped another two trillion won ($2.3 billion) into the banking system to prevent a credit squeeze sparked by a financial crisis at the Hanbo Group.
But industry analysts said debt defaults within the country's 14th largest industrial conglomerate has dealt a new blow to the nation's troubled banks.
It could result in higher interest rates and tighter credit to smaller companies, they said.

Last week Moody's Investor Service placed under review for possible downgrade the ratings of Korea Exchange Bank, Korea First Bank, and Cho Hung Bank, which have the biggest exposure to Hanbo, whose steel unit has crumbled.
"The crisis will hit the banks hard," said Kim Byung-suk, a banking analyst at Hannuri-Salomon Securities.
"The size of the loans these banks made to Hanbo was unprecedented -- not comparable to any other company."

Hanbo's steel subsidiary, which defaulted on debts last week, borrowed five trillion won ($5.8 billion) from banks and financial institutions, about 20 times its net worth, according to the finance ministry.
Hanbo Steel Co plans to file for court protection on Tuesday along with three other Hanbo Group affiliates.
The central bank flushed two trillion won into commercial banks by allowing them to cash in their Monetary Stabilisation Bonds ahead of maturity.
This follows an injection of one trillion won last Friday in the form of repurchase agreements.
Korea First Bank is the biggest creditor to Hanbo Steel with outstanding loans of 1.08 trillion won. Cho Hung Bank has loaned 494 billion won and Korea Exchange Bank 421 billion won.

Analysts said the Hanbo crisis would mean another bad year for banks, hammered by falling stock investments. Plunging share prices wiped 4.96 trillion won from the investment portfolios of the country's 25 commercial banks last year, according to central bank statistics.
Korea First Bank posted a net profit of 6.2 billion won last year, down 64.4 percent from 17.4 billion in 1995.
"Most likely it would face a net loss this year," said Kim.
Bank profits slumped by an average of 2.4 percent to a combined 846.8 billion won last year.
Analysts said Hanbo's default would force banks to be more cautious in giving out loans, and it would make it difficult for small companies to borrow.
"Banks will become picky on handing out loans and tighten the size," said one analyst at a Western brokerage.
Kim said: "There is a possibility local money market rates could go up as a result."
Moody's said its action reflected the continued deterioration in the asset quality of Korean banks.
It said the asset quality of Korea Exchange Bank, Korea First Bank and Cho Hung Bank -- among the big Seoul-based banks -- had suffered from decades of government-directed lending.
Yields on benchmark three-year corporate bonds have edged higher, closing on Monday at 12.07 percent against 12.05 percent last Wednesday before Hanbo Steel's default.

On Monday a group of 61 creditors to Hanbo Steel said it would support court receivership to keep the company afloat and would suspend demands for debt repayment and resume overdraft facilities once protection was granted.
"We will continue to provide funds to Hanbo Steel until its steel mill is completed in Tangjin," said Korea First Bank head Sheen Kwang-shik, who leads the group.
Sheen said creditors would also offer funds to Hanbo Steel's suppliers to prevent a chain reaction of bankruptcies.
